newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czechs to elect new Senate amid broad scepticism.
newsitem.headline: Czechs to elect new Senate amid broad scepticism.

text.p: Czechs go to the polls for the second time this year on Friday in Senate elections which are key to the future of the minority centre-right government.

With opinion surveys indicating many Czechs are sceptical about the need for the newly created upper house at all, President Vaclav Havel called on citizens to vote in high numbers for the sake of national stability.

"I firmly believe you will turn out for these elections in great numbers and the majority of you do understand the great significance of your vote," Havel said in a speech broadcast on the eve of the elections.
Voting in the first round starts nationwide at 2 p.m. (1300 GMT) on Friday and ends at the same time on Saturday.

The Senate, an institution which has not existed since before World War Two, would guarantee continuity and stability in the legislative branch of government and would mean that the public will was expressed more consistently, the president said.
Havel, who spent almost five years in communist jails in the fight to restore Czech democracy, regularly issues such appeals before elections.
Until now Czechs, who regained their pre-war democracy only after the 1989 fall of communism, have heeded his appeals. Turnout was 76.4 percent in lower house polls last June.
But the picture is less clear for the Senate polls, which end on November 22-23 with a top-two runoff in constituencies where no candidate won more than half the first round vote.
The Senate has few powers and its members are likely to be older, more reflective politicians as government and opposition leaders are all members of the lower house, the Chamber of Deputies.
Havel said it was important to have the 81-member upper house, elected by run-offs if needed, which can scrutinise legislation from the lower house, elected by proportional representation.

But opinion polls suggest this time Czechs may not heed his call for a high election turnout. A survey by the IVVM agency showed that only 57 percent planned to vote in the first round and 52 in the runoffs.

"There is, in general, low interest in the elections and the willingness to vote is low," said Eliska Rendlova of IVVM. Another survey showed 53 percent of those questioned doubted the need for a Senate.
Politicians have also been lukewarm. The Senate was written into the new constitution of the Czech Republic which came into force in 1993 after the breakup of Czechoslovakia.
Only now, almost four years later, is the Senate to be elected after much footdragging from both the centre-right and the centre-left of politics.

But politicians and pundits are eager to scrutinise the results to see how well the Civic Democratic Party (ODS) of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and its two junior coalition partners do after they narrowly lost their lower house majority in June.
If they do well, Klaus may be tempted to provoke early lower house elections in an attempt to regain the majority lost in a surge in support for the opposition Social Democrats.
But if the Social Democrats win the Senate race, Klaus might be forced to resign.

Most opinion polls suggest a tight race with ODS and Social Democrats neck and neck on about 26 percent support. However, the last survey published before a pre-election blackout came into force suggested the ODS was pulling ahead after an outbreak of squabbling in Social Democrat ranks.
The Social Democrats may also have suffered from a row this week over allegations by their chairman Milos Zeman that the state intelligence agency BIS had spied on him.
Havel, angered that Zeman offered no evidence to back up his claim, accused him of being extremely irresponsible.
